Caddy is an extensible server platform written in Go.

At its core, Caddy merely manages configuration. Modules are plugged
in statically at compile-time to provide useful functionality. Caddy's
standard distribution includes common modules to serve HTTP, TLS,
and PKI applications, including the automation of certificates.

To run Caddy, use:

	- 'caddy run' to run Caddy in the foreground (recommended).
	- 'caddy start' to start Caddy in the background; only do this
	  if you will be keeping the terminal window open until you run
	  'caddy stop' to close the server.

When Caddy is started, it opens a locally-bound administrative socket
to which configuration can be POSTed via a restful HTTP API (see
https://caddyserver.com/docs/api).

Caddy's native configuration format is JSON. However, config adapters
can be used to convert other config formats to JSON when Caddy receives
its configuration. The Caddyfile is a built-in config adapter that is
popular for hand-written configurations due to its straightforward
syntax (see https://caddyserver.com/docs/caddyfile). Many third-party
adapters are available (see https://caddyserver.com/docs/config-adapters).
Use 'caddy adapt' to see how a config translates to JSON.

For convenience, the CLI can act as an HTTP client to give Caddy its
initial configuration for you. If a file named Caddyfile is in the
current working directory, it will do this automatically. Otherwise,
you can use the --config flag to specify the path to a config file.

Some special-purpose subcommands build and load a configuration file
for you directly from command line input; for example:

	- caddy file-server
	- caddy reverse-proxy
	- caddy respond

These commands disable the administration endpoint because their
configuration is specified solely on the command line.

Caddy is an extensible server platform written in Go.

At its core, Caddy merely manages configuration. Modules are plugged
in statically at compile-time to provide useful functionality. Caddy's
standard distribution includes common modules to serve HTTP, TLS,
and PKI applications, including the automation of certificates.

To run Caddy, use:

	- 'caddy run' to run Caddy in the foreground (recommended).
	- 'caddy start' to start Caddy in the background; only do this
	  if you will be keeping the terminal window open until you run
	  'caddy stop' to close the server.

When Caddy is started, it opens a locally-bound administrative socket
to which configuration can be POSTed via a restful HTTP API (see
https://caddyserver.com/docs/api).

Caddy's native configuration format is JSON. However, config adapters
can be used to convert other config formats to JSON when Caddy receives
its configuration. The Caddyfile is a built-in config adapter that is
popular for hand-written configurations due to its straightforward
syntax (see https://caddyserver.com/docs/caddyfile). Many third-party
adapters are available (see https://caddyserver.com/docs/config-adapters).
Use 'caddy adapt' to see how a config translates to JSON.

For convenience, the CLI can act as an HTTP client to give Caddy its
initial configuration for you. If a file named Caddyfile is in the
current working directory, it will do this automatically. Otherwise,
you can use the --config flag to specify the path to a config file.

Some special-purpose subcommands build and load a configuration file
for you directly from command line input; for example:

	- caddy file-server
	- caddy reverse-proxy
	- caddy respond

These commands disable the administration endpoint because their
configuration is specified solely on the command line.

# caddy resource: agent guide

This binary is the Caddy web server with one extra HTTP handler, `resource`. You declare **resources**, one definition file per resource, in a directory. Each resource becomes a REST endpoint over PostgreSQL:

- `GET <path>`: paginated collection. `GET <path>/<identifier>`: one item.
- `POST <path>`: create. `PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE <path>/<identifier>`: replace, update, delete.
- Output is JSON-LD/Hydra by default (`member`, `totalItems`, `view`, `search`), or plain JSON, or CSV, chosen by the `Accept` header, `?format=csv` or a `.csv` suffix (`/books.csv`).
- Dedicated endpoints (reports, exports, actions) are declared with `operations`, e.g. `GET /business/export` always answering CSV.
- `GET /openapi.json`: OpenAPI 3.1 of every resource. `GET /`: entrypoint listing the resources.

A resource **reads** either a `table` as-is, or the result of a `query`: a TypeScript function returning parameterized SQL (or computed rows). It **writes** with generated `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` (table resources), or with a `command`: functions running inside a transaction, where business rules live. Query and command scripts are written in **TypeScript** (`.ts`) or in **Starlark** (`.star` or `.py`, a Python dialect); both get the same `ctx` API. Pagination, filters and item lookup are applied by the server on top of the table or the query. There is nothing to compile and nothing to install. Read this guide once, completely: it is the whole documentation.

2. Start the server once, in the background: `./caddy run > caddy.log 2>&1 &` (it reads `./Caddyfile`). It starts whatever the state of the definitions and **reloads the definitions directory by itself** within a second of any change: never restart it for a definition or script change (only for a `Caddyfile` change).
3. Write one definition file per resource in `resources/` (format below), plus the query and command scripts they reference.
4. Request your endpoints. While a definition is invalid, its paths answer its validation errors (`500` problem+json with `code`, `pointer`, `hint`, and `errors` listing all of them); other paths keep working, and unknown paths answer `404` listing the definitions that have errors. `./caddy resource validate --dir resources --dsn '<dsn>'` prints the full report offline. Fix errors in order.
5. Check the result with curl, e.g. `curl -s localhost:8080/books` and `curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/books -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"Dune"}'`.

## Caddyfile

```
{
	admin off
}

:8080 {
	resource {
		dir resources
		dsn postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/dbname
	}
}
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dir` | `resources` | Definitions directory, relative to the directory where `caddy` is started. Can also be given inline: `resource ./resources { ... }`. |
| `dsn` | `$DATABASE_URL` | PostgreSQL connection string. `{$VAR}` is replaced by an environment variable when the Caddyfile is read. |

The `resource` handler answers every request of the site: `/`, `/openapi.json`, `/contexts/<Name>`, and the resource paths; anything else is a `404` problem listing the available paths. `admin off` disables Caddy's admin API on port 2019 (remove it if you want `caddy reload`/`caddy stop`).

## Definition files

Every file directly inside the directory whose name ends in `.json` or `.ts` is a definition, except `*.query.ts`, `*.command.ts` (and their `.js` variants), `*.d.ts`, `package.json`, `tsconfig.json` and names starting with `.` or `_`. `.star` and `.py` files are always scripts, never definitions. Subdirectories are ignored. Name files after the resource (`Book.json`).

A JSON definition backed by a table, readable and writable with generated SQL:

```json
{
  "name": "Author",
  "path": "/authors",
  "table": "author",
  "properties": {
    "id": {"type": "integer", "identifier": true, "readOnly": true},
    "name": {"type": "string", "filterable": true, "required": true}
  }
}
```

The same in TypeScript (`Author.ts`). `defineResource` is a global identity function, there is nothing to import:

```ts
export default defineResource({
  name: "Author",
  path: "/authors",
  table: "author",
  properties: {
    id: { type: "integer", identifier: true, readOnly: true },
    name: { type: "string", filterable: true, required: true },
  },
});
```

A definition backed by a query, writable through a command (`Book.json` + `book.query.ts` + `book.command.ts`):

```json
{
  "name": "Book",
  "path": "/books",
  "query": "book.query.ts",
  "command": "book.command.ts",
  "itemsPerPage": 10,
  "input": {
    "title": {"type": "string", "required": true},
    "author_id": {"type": "integer", "required": true}
  },
  "properties": {
    "id": {"type": "integer", "identifier": true},
    "title": {"type": "string"},
    "author": {"type": "string", "filterable": true}
  }
}
```

`properties` is the output (what reads return); `input` is what writes accept. They differ here: a book is written with an `author_id` and read with the author's name.

### Keys

| Key | Required | Rules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | yes | PascalCase, singular: `Book`, `BookReview`. Used as JSON-LD `@type` and in `/contexts/<name>`. Unique. |
| `path` | yes, unless `operations` is set | Lowercase, leading slash, no trailing slash: `/books`, `/book-reviews`. Items live at `<path>/<identifier>`. Unique. Reserved: `/openapi.json`, `/contexts`, `/docs.jsonld`, `/errors`. |
| `table` | one of `table`/`query` | `table` or `schema.table`. Reads the declared properties as columns of that table; writes with generated SQL unless `command` is set. |
| `query` | one of `table`/`query` | Script in the same directory, no directory part: `<name>.query.ts` (TypeScript) or `<name>.star` / `<name>.py` (Starlark). See Queries. |
| `command` | no | Script in the same directory: `<name>.command.ts` or `<name>.star` / `<name>.py`. See Commands. Required to make a `query` resource writable; replaces the generated SQL of a `table` resource. |
| `input` | no | The request body accepted by `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH` (an input DTO): an object of field name to `{type, required, description}`. Without it, the body accepts the properties that are not `readOnly`. For a `table` resource without command, input names must be columns (the generated SQL writes them). |
| `readOnly` | no | `true` disables every write (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` answer `405`). |
| `formats` | no | Output formats allowed, among `"jsonld"`, `"json"`, `"csv"`. Default: all three; the first one is used when the client expresses no preference. |
| `operations` | no | Dedicated endpoints replacing the default CRUD endpoints. See Dedicated operations. |
| `allow` | no | `{"fetch": ["api.example.com", "127.0.0.1:9000"], "env": ["API_TOKEN"]}`: hosts (`host` or `host:port`) that `ctx.fetch` may call, environment variables that `ctx.env` may read. Everything else is denied. |
| `properties` | yes | Object of property name to property. Key order is output order (and CSV column order). **A property name is the column name**: the table must have a column with exactly that name, or the query must return a column with exactly that name. |
| `itemsPerPage` | no | Page size, 1 to 1000, default 30. |
| `description` | no | Free text, shown in OpenAPI. |

Property object:

| Key | Required | Rules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | yes | `string`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean` or `datetime`. |
| `identifier` | exactly one property (at most one with `operations`) | `true` on the property used in item URLs and for ordering. Its type must be `integer` or `string`. |
| `filterable` | no | `true` enables `?<property>=<value>` exact-match filtering on the collection. |
| `required` | no | `true`: must be present in `POST` and `PUT` bodies. |
| `readOnly` | no | `true`: output only, rejected in request bodies when the definition has no `input`. Use it for generated identifiers (serial) and computed columns. |
| `description` | no | Free text, shown in OpenAPI. |

Any other key is an error (`unknown_field`). Types and the PostgreSQL column types they accept:

| `type` | PostgreSQL columns | JSON |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `string` | text, varchar, char, uuid, name, enums, domains | string |
| `integer` | smallint, integer, bigint (serial too) | number without decimals |
| `number` | integer types, real, double precision, numeric | number |
| `boolean` | boolean | `true`/`false` |
| `datetime` | timestamp, timestamptz, date | RFC 3339 string in UTC, `"2024-01-31T12:00:00Z"`; input also accepts `"2024-01-31"` |

NULL is output as `null` for every type. A mismatch is a `type_mismatch` error: change the declared type, or cast in the query (`price::float8 AS price`, `created_at::text AS created_at`).

To expose only some rows, rename a column, compute a value or join tables, use a `query`: `table` cannot do any of that.

## Queries

A query module default-exports a function receiving a context and returning SQL built with the `ctx.sql` tagged template:

```ts
export default function query(ctx: QueryContext): Sql {
  return ctx.sql`
    SELECT b.id, b.title, a.name AS author
    FROM book b
    JOIN author a ON a.id = b.author_id
    WHERE b.published`;
}
```

The SQL you return is wrapped by the server, exactly like this (`r` is the alias of your query):

```sql
-- collection, page N, with ?author=... applied
SELECT * FROM (<your query>) r WHERE r."author" = $1 ORDER BY r."id" LIMIT <itemsPerPage> OFFSET <(N-1)*itemsPerPage>
SELECT count(*) FROM (<your query>) r WHERE r."author" = $1
-- item GET /books/7 (also used before PUT/PATCH/DELETE and to read back after a write)
SELECT * FROM (<your query>) r WHERE r."id" = $1
```

Consequences:

- Return **one `SELECT`** (`WITH ... SELECT` works too). No `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` (pagination is added), no `ORDER BY` (collections are always sorted by the identifier, ascending). A trailing `;` is tolerated.
- Return one column per declared property, **named exactly like the property**. Use `AS` to rename: `a.name AS author`. PostgreSQL folds unquoted names to lower case: a property `authorName` needs `AS "authorName"` (double quotes); snake_case property names avoid the problem. Extra columns are allowed and ignored. Two columns with the same name (`b.id, a.id`) are an error: alias one of them.
- Rows excluded by your `WHERE` exist nowhere: not in the collection, not as items (`404`), and they cannot be updated or deleted (`404`).
- Filters apply to the columns your query returns, so a joined or computed column can be `filterable` (`author` above, filtered with `?author=Frank%20Herbert`).

### Queries that return rows

When the data does not come from SQL (a remote API, computed values), the query function returns rows instead of `ctx.sql`. The server can no longer paginate or filter for you, so it tells the function what is asked through `ctx.operation`:

- `ctx.operation === "collection"`: honor `ctx.page` (1-based), `ctx.itemsPerPage` and `ctx.filters` (object of filterable property to the requested value, already converted to the property type), and return `{ items: [...rows of that page], totalItems: <rows across all pages> }`.
- `ctx.operation === "item"`: return the row whose identifier equals `ctx.id` (already converted to the identifier type), or `null` for a 404.

Each row is an object with every declared property, values of the declared type (`invalid_row` otherwise). The function may be `async` and `await` `ctx.fetch`:

```ts
export default async function query(ctx: QueryContext) {
  const res = await ctx.fetch("https://api.example.com/quotes");
  let rows = (await res.json()).map((q) => ({ id: q.id, text: q.body, author: q.by }));
  if (ctx.operation === "item") return rows.find((r) => r.id === ctx.id) ?? null;
  if (ctx.filters.author !== undefined) rows = rows.filter((r) => r.author === ctx.filters.author);
  const start = (ctx.page - 1) * ctx.itemsPerPage;
  return { items: rows.slice(start, start + ctx.itemsPerPage), totalItems: rows.length };
}
```

with `"allow": {"fetch": ["api.example.com"]}` in the definition.

## Commands

Writes go through a **command**. Without a `command` file, a `table` resource gets generated SQL: `POST` runs `INSERT INTO <table> (<body keys>) VALUES (...) RETURNING <identifier>`, `PUT`/`PATCH` run `UPDATE <table> SET <body keys> WHERE <identifier> = <id>`, `DELETE` runs `DELETE FROM <table> WHERE <identifier> = <id>`. A `query` resource without a command is read-only.

A command module exports one function per operation it supports; a missing function makes that method answer `405`:

| Export | HTTP | Receives | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `create(input, ctx)` | `POST <path>` | the validated body | **the identifier of the new row** (required) |
| `update(input, ctx)` | `PUT`/`PATCH <path>/<id>` | the validated body (`PATCH`: only the keys sent); `ctx.id` is the identifier | nothing |
| `remove(input, ctx)` | `DELETE <path>/<id>` | `{}`; `ctx.id` is the identifier | nothing |

(`delete` is a reserved word in JavaScript, so the delete function is exported as `remove`.)

```ts
export function create(input, ctx) {
  const [author] = ctx.db.query(ctx.sql`SELECT name FROM author WHERE id = ${input.author_id}`);
  if (!author) {
    ctx.reject({ message: `author ${input.author_id} does not exist`, pointer: "/author_id", hint: "Create the author first with POST /authors." });
  }
  const [row] = ctx.db.query(ctx.sql`INSERT INTO book (title, author_id) VALUES (${input.title}, ${input.author_id}) RETURNING id`);
  return row.id;
}

export function update(input, ctx) {
  if ("title" in input) ctx.db.exec(ctx.sql`UPDATE book SET title = ${input.title} WHERE id = ${ctx.id}`);
}

export function remove(input, ctx) {
  ctx.db.exec(ctx.sql`DELETE FROM book WHERE id = ${ctx.id}`);
}
```

Lifecycle of a write:

1. The body is validated against `input` (or, without `input`, the non-`readOnly` properties) before any code runs: unknown keys (`unknown_property`), `readOnly` properties (`read_only_property`), wrong types (`invalid_property_value`), missing `required` fields on `POST`/`PUT` (`required_property`). JSON-LD keys (`@id`, `@type`, `@context`) are ignored. Values reach the command already typed (integers are numbers, datetimes RFC 3339 strings).
2. For `PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE`, the item is first looked up through the query: invisible items are `404`.
3. The command (or the generated SQL) runs **inside one transaction**: everything done with `ctx.db` commits together, or rolls back if the function throws, calls `ctx.reject`, or a statement fails. Database constraint errors become `409 conflict`, `422 invalid_reference` or `422 constraint_violation` with a pointer to the column.
4. The written row is **read back through the query**, so responses always have the read shape: `201` + `Location` header + the item for `POST`, `200` + the item for `PUT`/`PATCH`, `204` without body for `DELETE`. If the query does not return the written row (its `WHERE` excludes it), `POST` answers `201` with the `Location` header and no body, `PUT`/`PATCH` answer `204`.

To refuse an input for a business reason, call `ctx.reject({ message, pointer, hint, code, status })`: it stops the command, rolls back, and answers a problem with HTTP `status` (default `422`) and `code` (default `rejected`). `pointer` is a JSON pointer into the body (`/author_id`). A plain `throw new Error(...)` is treated as a bug: `500 script_error`.

## Dedicated operations

A report or an action is often just an endpoint, not a representation of a resource. `operations` declares such endpoints; when present, it **replaces** the default `GET <path>`, `POST <path>`, `GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE <path>/<id>` endpoints, and `path` and the identifier become optional. `properties` still describes the rows (CSV header, JSON keys, body validation).

```json
{
  "name": "AuthorReport",
  "operations": [
    {"method": "GET", "path": "/business/export", "format": "csv", "query": "author_report.query.ts"}
  ],
  "properties": {
    "author": {"type": "string", "filterable": true},
    "books": {"type": "integer"}
  }
}
```

| Operation key | Required | Rules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `method` | yes | `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` (upper case). |
| `path` | yes | Full path, lowercase, no placeholders: `/business/export`. Unique with its method across all definitions. |
| `format` | no | `jsonld` (default), `json` or `csv`. **Pinned**: `Accept`, `?format` and suffixes are ignored. |
| `query` | for `GET`, unless the definition has `query` or `table` | Query script of this operation. |
| `command` | for other methods, unless the definition has `command` | Command script; the function called is `create` for `POST`, `update` for `PUT`/`PATCH`, `remove` for `DELETE`. |
| `input` | no | Input of this operation, same syntax as the definition's `input`. |
| `description` | no | Shown in OpenAPI. |

A `GET` operation behaves like a collection: filters on `filterable` properties, `?page=N` pagination (JSON-LD and JSON), and CSV returns **every row** unless `?page` is given. Without an identifier there is no ordering added: an `ORDER BY` in your query is kept. A write operation validates the JSON body against its own `input` (an operation key, same syntax), else the definition's `input`, else the non-`readOnly` properties, runs its command in a transaction, and answers the row the command returns (`201` for `POST`, `200` otherwise), or `204` when it returns nothing.

## Host API (`ctx`), shared by queries and commands

| Member | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ``ctx.sql`...` `` | tagged template returning `Sql` | Every `${value}` becomes a bind parameter (`$1`, `$2`, ...), never concatenated text, so it is injection-safe. Values: string, number, boolean, `null`/`undefined` (SQL NULL), arrays of one scalar type (a PostgreSQL array, use `= ANY(${ids})`), or another ``ctx.sql`...` `` fragment, which is inlined with its own parameters. Table and column names cannot be interpolated. |
| `ctx.db.query(sql)` | `Row[]` | Runs a `ctx.sql` statement and returns its rows as plain objects (use `RETURNING` to get values back from `INSERT`/`UPDATE`). Synchronous. Inside a command it runs in the command's transaction. |
| `ctx.db.exec(sql)` | `{ rowCount }` | Runs a `ctx.sql` statement without returning rows. Synchronous. Passing a plain string is an error. |
| `ctx.fetch(url, { method, headers, body })` | `{ status, ok, headers, text(), json() }` | HTTP request to a host listed in `allow.fetch` (`fetch_denied` otherwise). `body` may be a string or an object (sent as JSON). Non-2xx statuses do not throw: check `res.ok`. Synchronous under the hood; `await` works. 5 second timeout. |
| `ctx.env(name)` | `string` | Environment variable listed in `allow.env` (`env_denied` otherwise); `""` when unset. For secrets such as API tokens. |
| `ctx.reject({ message, pointer?, hint?, code?, status? })` | never returns | Refuses the request with a 4xx problem (commands). |
| `ctx.request.method` / `ctx.request.path` | string | HTTP method and path of the request (`"GET"`, `"/books/7"`). |
| `ctx.request.query(name)` | `string \| null` | First value of a URL query parameter, `null` when absent. |
| `ctx.request.header(name)` | `string \| null` | Request header, case-insensitive, `null` when absent. |
| `ctx.operation` | string | `"collection"`, `"item"`, `"create"`, `"update"` or `"delete"`. |
| `ctx.id` | `number \| string \| null` | Identifier of the item being read, updated or deleted. |
| `ctx.page`, `ctx.itemsPerPage`, `ctx.filters` | number, number, object | Collection requests only (see Queries that return rows). |

Request values are strings: cast them in SQL when comparing with non-text columns, otherwise PostgreSQL may fail to infer the type (`query_failed`):

```ts
export default function query(ctx: QueryContext): Sql {
  const since = ctx.request.query("since");
  const cond = since === null ? ctx.sql`` : ctx.sql`AND b.year >= ${since}::int`;
  return ctx.sql`SELECT b.id, b.title, b.year FROM book b WHERE b.tenant = ${ctx.request.header("x-tenant")} ${cond}`;
}
```

Query parameters that are neither `page` nor a property name are ignored by the server and left to your query (`since` above). Scripts have no other I/O: no imports (except `import { defineResource } from "caddy-resource"`, never needed), no Node.js API, no timers. Type annotations are stripped without type checking; `QueryContext` and `Sql` need no import. A script call must finish within 10 seconds.

The query function also runs during validation (`caddy resource validate`, startup, every reload) as a collection request for page 1 with an empty request: no query parameters, no headers (`query()`/`header()` return `null`), `ctx.filters` empty. I/O is switched off there: when the function returns `ctx.sql`, its columns and types are checked with a `LIMIT 0` query; when it calls `ctx.fetch`, `ctx.db.query` or `ctx.db.exec`, validation stops at that call and checks nothing more, and the rows it returns are validated on each request instead (`invalid_row`). Commands are never run during validation.

## Starlark scripts (`.star`, `.py`)

Starlark is Python without `import`, classes, exceptions (`try`/`except`/`raise`), f-strings, `with`, `async` and the `is` operator; each of those is reported with what to write instead. Strings use `%` or `.format()`, `None` is compared with `==`. The `ctx` API is the same, in snake_case, and every call is synchronous:

| TypeScript | Starlark |
| --- | --- |
| `export default function query(ctx)` | `def query(ctx):` |
| `export function create(input, ctx)` / `update` / `remove` | `def create(input, ctx):` / `def update(input, ctx):` / `def remove(input, ctx):` (`def delete` works too) |
| ``ctx.sql`... ${a} ... ${b}` `` | `ctx.sql("... {a} ... {b}", a = x, b = y)`: each `{name}` binds the keyword argument of that name (write `/` for literal braces); positional `ctx.sql("... $1 ... $2", x, y)` also works. A value may be another `ctx.sql(...)` fragment |
| `ctx.db.query(sql)` / `ctx.db.exec(sql).rowCount` | `ctx.db.query(sql)` / `ctx.db.exec(sql).row_count` |
| `await ctx.fetch(url, {method, headers, body})` | `ctx.fetch(url, method = "POST", headers = {...}, body = {...})` |
| `res.status`, `res.ok`, `res.headers`, `res.json()`, `res.text()` | same |
| `JSON.parse(s)` / `JSON.stringify(v)` | `ctx.json.decode(s)` / `ctx.json.encode(v)` |
| `ctx.env(name)`, `ctx.request.query(name)`, `ctx.request.header(name)` | same (`None` when absent) |
| `ctx.reject({message, pointer, hint, code, status})` | `ctx.reject("message", pointer = "/field", hint = "...", code = "...", status = 409)` |
| `ctx.itemsPerPage`, `{items, totalItems}` | `ctx.items_per_page`, `{"items": [...], "total_items": n}` (`"totalItems"` also accepted) |

```python
def query(ctx):
    res = ctx.fetch("https://api.example.com/quotes")
    rows = [{"id": q["id"], "text": q["body"], "author": q["by"]} for q in res.json()]
    if ctx.operation == "item":
        for r in rows:
            if r["id"] == ctx.id:
                return r
        return None
    if "author" in ctx.filters:
        rows = [r for r in rows if r["author"] == ctx.filters["author"]]
    start = (ctx.page - 1) * ctx.items_per_page
    return {"items": rows[start:start + ctx.items_per_page], "total_items": len(rows)}
```

```python
def create(input, ctx):
    authors = ctx.db.query(ctx.sql("SELECT name FROM author WHERE id = {id}", id = input["author_id"]))
    if len(authors) == 0:
        ctx.reject("author %d does not exist" % input["author_id"], pointer = "/author_id")
    rows = ctx.db.query(ctx.sql("INSERT INTO book (title, author_id) VALUES ({title}, {author_id}) RETURNING id", title = input["title"], author_id = input["author_id"]))
    return rows[0]["id"]
```

## HTTP API produced

Collection, `GET /books?page=2`:

```json
{
  "@context": "/contexts/Book",
  "@id": "/books",
  "@type": "Collection",
  "totalItems": 12,
  "member": [
    {"@id": "/books/11", "@type": "Book", "id": 11, "title": "Dune", "author": "Frank Herbert"}
  ],
  "view": {"@id": "/books?page=2", "@type": "PartialCollectionView", "first": "/books?page=1", "last": "/books?page=2", "previous": "/books?page=1"},
  "search": {"@type": "IriTemplate", "template": "/books{?author}", "variableRepresentation": "BasicRepresentation", "mapping": [{"@type": "IriTemplateMapping", "variable": "author", "property": "author", "required": false}]}
}
```

- `?page=N` selects a page (1-based); a page after the last one returns an empty `member`. `view` appears when there is more than one page or a filter is applied; `search` when a property is filterable.
- `?<property>=<value>` filters on a `filterable` property (exact, case-sensitive match; several filters are combined with AND). Booleans are `true`/`false`, datetimes RFC 3339 or `YYYY-MM-DD`. A non-filterable property is `400 filter_not_enabled`.
- Item, `GET /books/11`: the member object plus `"@context": "/contexts/Book"`.
- There is no sorting parameter and no partial match.

Output formats are chosen, in this order, by a path suffix (`/books.csv`, `/books/7.json`, `.jsonld`), by `?format=jsonld|json|csv`, then by `Accept` (first supported type wins; none or `*/*` gives the first allowed format). A format the resource does not allow (see `formats`) is `406 not_acceptable`, listing the allowed ones.

| Format | Media type | Item | Collection |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `jsonld` (default) | `application/ld+json` | JSON-LD object | Hydra collection above |
| `json` | `application/json` | object with the properties only | array of those objects (no total, no links; use `?page=`) |
| `csv` | `text/csv` | header row + one row | header row (property names, declaration order) + **every matching row** (filters apply; no pagination unless `?page=N` is given), streamed; NULL is an empty field; sent with `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="<path>.csv"` |

Request bodies are JSON only: `Content-Type: application/json`, `application/ld+json` or `application/merge-patch+json` with one JSON object (`415` otherwise; CSV is an output format).

Errors are `application/problem+json`:

```json
{"type": "/errors/422", "title": "An error occurred", "status": 422, "detail": "\"titel\" is not a property of Book", "code": "unknown_property", "hint": "Did you mean \"title\"? The body is validated against \"input\". Accepted keys: title, author_id.", "resource": "Book", "pointer": "/titel"}
```

When several input errors are found, the first is described at the top level and all of them are listed in an `errors` array (`code`, `pointer`, `message`, `hint` each).

## Validation errors

`caddy resource validate` prints, and exits with status 1 when `valid` is false:

```json
{"valid": false, "errors": [{"code": "unknown_column", "resource": "Book", "pointer": "/properties/author", "message": "column \"author\" is not returned by the query", "hint": "Query returns: id, title, author_name. Alias the column in the SELECT (expr AS author) or rename the property."}], "warnings": []}
```

`resource` is the definition `name` (the file name when the name is unknown), `pointer` is a JSON pointer into that definition. Checks run in this order: JSON syntax / TypeScript compilation, schema, identifier, `table` xor `query`, query and command files and their exports, then, with a dsn, against the database: the table exists, the query runs (empty request), each property is a returned column (or row key), each column type matches. `caddy run` and `caddy validate` do not fail on invalid definitions (only on `Caddyfile` errors such as a missing `dsn`): the server logs the report as a warning and serves the errors on the affected paths.

### Error codes

1	# caddy resource: agent guide
2	
3	This binary is the Caddy web server with one extra HTTP handler, `resource`. You declare **resources**, one definition file per resource, in a directory. Each resource becomes a REST endpoint over PostgreSQL:
4	
5	- `GET <path>`: paginated collection. `GET <path>/<identifier>`: one item.
6	- `POST <path>`: create. `PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE <path>/<identifier>`: replace, update, delete.
7	- Output is JSON-LD/Hydra by default (`member`, `totalItems`, `view`, `search`), or plain JSON, or CSV, chosen by the `Accept` header, `?format=csv` or a `.csv` suffix (`/books.csv`).
8	- Dedicated endpoints (reports, exports, actions) are declared with `operations`, e.g. `GET /business/export` always answering CSV.
9	- `GET /openapi.json`: OpenAPI 3.1 of every resource. `GET /`: entrypoint listing the resources.
10	
11	A resource **reads** either a `table` as-is, or the result of a `query`: a TypeScript function returning parameterized SQL (or computed rows). It **writes** with generated `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` (table resources), or with a `command`: functions running inside a transaction, where business rules live. Query and command scripts are written in **TypeScript** (`.ts`) or in **Starlark** (`.star` or `.py`, a Python dialect); both get the same `ctx` API. Pagination, filters and item lookup are applied by the server on top of the table or the query. There is nothing to compile and nothing to install. Read this guide once, completely: it is the whole documentation.
12	
13	## Workflow
14	
15	1. `./caddy resource init` scaffolds a `Caddyfile` and a `resources/` directory with one working example (optional).
16	2. Start the server once, in the background: `./caddy run > caddy.log 2>&1 &` (it reads `./Caddyfile`). It starts whatever the state of the definitions and **reloads the definitions directory by itself** within a second of any change: never restart it for a definition or script change (only for a `Caddyfile` change).
17	3. Write one definition file per resource in `resources/` (format below), plus the query and command scripts they reference.
18	4. Request your endpoints. While a definition is invalid, its paths answer its validation errors (`500` problem+json with `code`, `pointer`, `hint`, and `errors` listing all of them); other paths keep working, and unknown paths answer `404` listing the definitions that have errors. `./caddy resource validate --dir resources --dsn '<dsn>'` prints the full report offline. Fix errors in order.
19	5. Check the result with curl, e.g. `curl -s localhost:8080/books` and `curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/books -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"Dune"}'`.

21	## Caddyfile
22	
23	```
24	{
25		admin off
26	}
27	
28	:8080 {
29		resource {
30			dir resources
31			dsn postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/dbname
32		}
33	}
34	```
35	
36	| Option | Default | Meaning |
37	| --- | --- | --- |
38	| `dir` | `resources` | Definitions directory, relative to the directory where `caddy` is started. Can also be given inline: `resource ./resources { ... }`. |
39	| `dsn` | `$DATABASE_URL` | PostgreSQL connection string. `{$VAR}` is replaced by an environment variable when the Caddyfile is read. |
40	
41	The `resource` handler answers every request of the site: `/`, `/openapi.json`, `/contexts/<Name>`, and the resource paths; anything else is a `404` problem listing the available paths. `admin off` disables Caddy's admin API on port 2019 (remove it if you want `caddy reload`/`caddy stop`).

43	## Definition files
44	
45	Every file directly inside the directory whose name ends in `.json` or `.ts` is a definition, except `*.query.ts`, `*.command.ts` (and their `.js` variants), `*.d.ts`, `package.json`, `tsconfig.json` and names starting with `.` or `_`. `.star` and `.py` files are always scripts, never definitions. Subdirectories are ignored. Name files after the resource (`Book.json`).
46	
47	A JSON definition backed by a table, readable and writable with generated SQL:
48	
49	```json
50	{
51	  "name": "Author",
52	  "path": "/authors",
53	  "table": "author",
54	  "properties": {
55	    "id": {"type": "integer", "identifier": true, "readOnly": true},
56	    "name": {"type": "string", "filterable": true, "required": true}
57	  }
58	}
59	```
60	
61	The same in TypeScript (`Author.ts`). `defineResource` is a global identity function, there is nothing to import:
62	
63	```ts
64	export default defineResource({
65	  name: "Author",
66	  path: "/authors",
67	  table: "author",
68	  properties: {
69	    id: { type: "integer", identifier: true, readOnly: true },
70	    name: { type: "string", filterable: true, required: true },
71	  },
72	});
73	```
74	
75	A definition backed by a query, writable through a command (`Book.json` + `book.query.ts` + `book.command.ts`):
76	
77	```json
78	{
79	  "name": "Book",
80	  "path": "/books",
81	  "query": "book.query.ts",
82	  "command": "book.command.ts",
83	  "itemsPerPage": 10,
84	  "input": {
85	    "title": {"type": "string", "required": true},
86	    "author_id": {"type": "integer", "required": true}
87	  },
88	  "properties": {
89	    "id": {"type": "integer", "identifier": true},
90	    "title": {"type": "string"},
91	    "author": {"type": "string", "filterable": true}
92	  }
93	}
94	```
95	
96	`properties` is the output (what reads return); `input` is what writes accept. They differ here: a book is written with an `author_id` and read with the author's name.
97	
98	### Keys
99	
100	| Key | Required | Rules |
101	| --- | --- | --- |
102	| `name` | yes | PascalCase, singular: `Book`, `BookReview`. Used as JSON-LD `@type` and in `/contexts/<name>`. Unique. |
103	| `path` | yes, unless `operations` is set | Lowercase, leading slash, no trailing slash: `/books`, `/book-reviews`. Items live at `<path>/<identifier>`. Unique. Reserved: `/openapi.json`, `/contexts`, `/docs.jsonld`, `/errors`. |
104	| `table` | one of `table`/`query` | `table` or `schema.table`. Reads the declared properties as columns of that table; writes with generated SQL unless `command` is set. |
105	| `query` | one of `table`/`query` | Script in the same directory, no directory part: `<name>.query.ts` (TypeScript) or `<name>.star` / `<name>.py` (Starlark). See Queries. |
106	| `command` | no | Script in the same directory: `<name>.command.ts` or `<name>.star` / `<name>.py`. See Commands. Required to make a `query` resource writable; replaces the generated SQL of a `table` resource. |
107	| `input` | no | The request body accepted by `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH` (an input DTO): an object of field name to `{type, required, description}`. Without it, the body accepts the properties that are not `readOnly`. For a `table` resource without command, input names must be columns (the generated SQL writes them). |
108	| `readOnly` | no | `true` disables every write (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` answer `405`). |
109	| `formats` | no | Output formats allowed, among `"jsonld"`, `"json"`, `"csv"`. Default: all three; the first one is used when the client expresses no preference. |
110	| `operations` | no | Dedicated endpoints replacing the default CRUD endpoints. See Dedicated operations. |
111	| `allow` | no | `{"fetch": ["api.example.com", "127.0.0.1:9000"], "env": ["API_TOKEN"]}`: hosts (`host` or `host:port`) that `ctx.fetch` may call, environment variables that `ctx.env` may read. Everything else is denied. |
112	| `properties` | yes | Object of property name to property. Key order is output order (and CSV column order). **A property name is the column name**: the table must have a column with exactly that name, or the query must return a column with exactly that name. |
113	| `itemsPerPage` | no | Page size, 1 to 1000, default 30. |
114	| `description` | no | Free text, shown in OpenAPI. |
115	
116	Property object:
117	
118	| Key | Required | Rules |
119	| --- | --- | --- |
120	| `type` | yes | `string`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean` or `datetime`. |
121	| `identifier` | exactly one property (at most one with `operations`) | `true` on the property used in item URLs and for ordering. Its type must be `integer` or `string`. |
122	| `filterable` | no | `true` enables `?<property>=<value>` exact-match filtering on the collection. |
123	| `required` | no | `true`: must be present in `POST` and `PUT` bodies. |
124	| `readOnly` | no | `true`: output only, rejected in request bodies when the definition has no `input`. Use it for generated identifiers (serial) and computed columns. |
125	| `description` | no | Free text, shown in OpenAPI. |
126	
127	Any other key is an error (`unknown_field`). Types and the PostgreSQL column types they accept:
128	
129	| `type` | PostgreSQL columns | JSON |
130	| --- | --- | --- |
131	| `string` | text, varchar, char, uuid, name, enums, domains | string |
132	| `integer` | smallint, integer, bigint (serial too) | number without decimals |
133	| `number` | integer types, real, double precision, numeric | number |
134	| `boolean` | boolean | `true`/`false` |
135	| `datetime` | timestamp, timestamptz, date | RFC 3339 string in UTC, `"2024-01-31T12:00:00Z"`; input also accepts `"2024-01-31"` |
136	
137	NULL is output as `null` for every type. A mismatch is a `type_mismatch` error: change the declared type, or cast in the query (`price::float8 AS price`, `created_at::text AS created_at`).
138	
139	To expose only some rows, rename a column, compute a value or join tables, use a `query`: `table` cannot do any of that.
140	
141	## Queries
142	
143	A query module default-exports a function receiving a context and returning SQL built with the `ctx.sql` tagged template:
144	
145	```ts
146	export default function query(ctx: QueryContext): Sql {
147	  return ctx.sql`
148	    SELECT b.id, b.title, a.name AS author
149	    FROM book b
150	    JOIN author a ON a.id = b.author_id
151	    WHERE b.published`;
152	}
153	```
154	
155	The SQL you return is wrapped by the server, exactly like this (`r` is the alias of your query):
156	
157	```sql
158	-- collection, page N, with ?author=... applied
159	SELECT * FROM (<your query>) r WHERE r."author" = $1 ORDER BY r."id" LIMIT <itemsPerPage> OFFSET <(N-1)*itemsPerPage>
160	SELECT count(*) FROM (<your query>) r WHERE r."author" = $1
161	-- item GET /books/7 (also used before PUT/PATCH/DELETE and to read back after a write)
162	SELECT * FROM (<your query>) r WHERE r."id" = $1
163	```
164	
165	Consequences:
166	
167	- Return **one `SELECT`** (`WITH ... SELECT` works too). No `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` (pagination is added), no `ORDER BY` (collections are always sorted by the identifier, ascending). A trailing `;` is tolerated.
168	- Return one column per declared property, **named exactly like the property**. Use `AS` to rename: `a.name AS author`. PostgreSQL folds unquoted names to lower case: a property `authorName` needs `AS "authorName"` (double quotes); snake_case property names avoid the problem. Extra columns are allowed and ignored. Two columns with the same name (`b.id, a.id`) are an error: alias one of them.
169	- Rows excluded by your `WHERE` exist nowhere: not in the collection, not as items (`404`), and they cannot be updated or deleted (`404`).
170	- Filters apply to the columns your query returns, so a joined or computed column can be `filterable` (`author` above, filtered with `?author=Frank%20Herbert`).
171	
172	### Queries that return rows
173	
174	When the data does not come from SQL (a remote API, computed values), the query function returns rows instead of `ctx.sql`. The server can no longer paginate or filter for you, so it tells the function what is asked through `ctx.operation`:
175	
176	- `ctx.operation === "collection"`: honor `ctx.page` (1-based), `ctx.itemsPerPage` and `ctx.filters` (object of filterable property to the requested value, already converted to the property type), and return `{ items: [...rows of that page], totalItems: <rows across all pages> }`.
177	- `ctx.operation === "item"`: return the row whose identifier equals `ctx.id` (already converted to the identifier type), or `null` for a 404.
178	
179	Each row is an object with every declared property, values of the declared type (`invalid_row` otherwise). The function may be `async` and `await` `ctx.fetch`:
180	
181	```ts
182	export default async function query(ctx: QueryContext) {
183	  const res = await ctx.fetch("https://api.example.com/quotes");
184	  let rows = (await res.json()).map((q) => ({ id: q.id, text: q.body, author: q.by }));
185	  if (ctx.operation === "item") return rows.find((r) => r.id === ctx.id) ?? null;
186	  if (ctx.filters.author !== undefined) rows = rows.filter((r) => r.author === ctx.filters.author);
187	  const start = (ctx.page - 1) * ctx.itemsPerPage;
188	  return { items: rows.slice(start, start + ctx.itemsPerPage), totalItems: rows.length };
189	}
190	```
191	
192	with `"allow": {"fetch": ["api.example.com"]}` in the definition.
193	
194	## Commands
195	
196	Writes go through a **command**. Without a `command` file, a `table` resource gets generated SQL: `POST` runs `INSERT INTO <table> (<body keys>) VALUES (...) RETURNING <identifier>`, `PUT`/`PATCH` run `UPDATE <table> SET <body keys> WHERE <identifier> = <id>`, `DELETE` runs `DELETE FROM <table> WHERE <identifier> = <id>`. A `query` resource without a command is read-only.
197	
198	A command module exports one function per operation it supports; a missing function makes that method answer `405`:
199	
200	| Export | HTTP | Receives | Returns |
201	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
202	| `create(input, ctx)` | `POST <path>` | the validated body | **the identifier of the new row** (required) |
203	| `update(input, ctx)` | `PUT`/`PATCH <path>/<id>` | the validated body (`PATCH`: only the keys sent); `ctx.id` is the identifier | nothing |
204	| `remove(input, ctx)` | `DELETE <path>/<id>` | `{}`; `ctx.id` is the identifier | nothing |
205	
206	(`delete` is a reserved word in JavaScript, so the delete function is exported as `remove`.)
207	
208	```ts
209	export function create(input, ctx) {
210	  const [author] = ctx.db.query(ctx.sql`SELECT name FROM author WHERE id = ${input.author_id}`);
211	  if (!author) {
212	    ctx.reject({ message: `author ${input.author_id} does not exist`, pointer: "/author_id", hint: "Create the author first with POST /authors." });
213	  }
214	  const [row] = ctx.db.query(ctx.sql`INSERT INTO book (title, author_id) VALUES (${input.title}, ${input.author_id}) RETURNING id`);
215	  return row.id;
216	}
217	
218	export function update(input, ctx) {
219	  if ("title" in input) ctx.db.exec(ctx.sql`UPDATE book SET title = ${input.title} WHERE id = ${ctx.id}`);
220	}
221	
222	export function remove(input, ctx) {
223	  ctx.db.exec(ctx.sql`DELETE FROM book WHERE id = ${ctx.id}`);
224	}
225	```
226	
227	Lifecycle of a write:
228	
229	1. The body is validated against `input` (or, without `input`, the non-`readOnly` properties) before any code runs: unknown keys (`unknown_property`), `readOnly` properties (`read_only_property`), wrong types (`invalid_property_value`), missing `required` fields on `POST`/`PUT` (`required_property`). JSON-LD keys (`@id`, `@type`, `@context`) are ignored. Values reach the command already typed (integers are numbers, datetimes RFC 3339 strings).
230	2. For `PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE`, the item is first looked up through the query: invisible items are `404`.
231	3. The command (or the generated SQL) runs **inside one transaction**: everything done with `ctx.db` commits together, or rolls back if the function throws, calls `ctx.reject`, or a statement fails. Database constraint errors become `409 conflict`, `422 invalid_reference` or `422 constraint_violation` with a pointer to the column.
232	4. The written row is **read back through the query**, so responses always have the read shape: `201` + `Location` header + the item for `POST`, `200` + the item for `PUT`/`PATCH`, `204` without body for `DELETE`. If the query does not return the written row (its `WHERE` excludes it), `POST` answers `201` with the `Location` header and no body, `PUT`/`PATCH` answer `204`.
233	
234	To refuse an input for a business reason, call `ctx.reject({ message, pointer, hint, code, status })`: it stops the command, rolls back, and answers a problem with HTTP `status` (default `422`) and `code` (default `rejected`). `pointer` is a JSON pointer into the body (`/author_id`). A plain `throw new Error(...)` is treated as a bug: `500 script_error`.
235	
236	## Dedicated operations
237	
238	A report or an action is often just an endpoint, not a representation of a resource. `operations` declares such endpoints; when present, it **replaces** the default `GET <path>`, `POST <path>`, `GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE <path>/<id>` endpoints, and `path` and the identifier become optional. `properties` still describes the rows (CSV header, JSON keys, body validation).
239	
240	```json
241	{
242	  "name": "AuthorReport",
243	  "operations": [
244	    {"method": "GET", "path": "/business/export", "format": "csv", "query": "author_report.query.ts"}
245	  ],
246	  "properties": {
247	    "author": {"type": "string", "filterable": true},
248	    "books": {"type": "integer"}
249	  }
250	}
251	```
252	
253	| Operation key | Required | Rules |
254	| --- | --- | --- |
255	| `method` | yes | `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` (upper case). |
256	| `path` | yes | Full path, lowercase, no placeholders: `/business/export`. Unique with its method across all definitions. |
257	| `format` | no | `jsonld` (default), `json` or `csv`. **Pinned**: `Accept`, `?format` and suffixes are ignored. |
258	| `query` | for `GET`, unless the definition has `query` or `table` | Query script of this operation. |
259	| `command` | for other methods, unless the definition has `command` | Command script; the function called is `create` for `POST`, `update` for `PUT`/`PATCH`, `remove` for `DELETE`. |
260	| `input` | no | Input of this operation, same syntax as the definition's `input`. |
261	| `description` | no | Shown in OpenAPI. |
262	
263	A `GET` operation behaves like a collection: filters on `filterable` properties, `?page=N` pagination (JSON-LD and JSON), and CSV returns **every row** unless `?page` is given. Without an identifier there is no ordering added: an `ORDER BY` in your query is kept. A write operation validates the JSON body against its own `input` (an operation key, same syntax), else the definition's `input`, else the non-`readOnly` properties, runs its command in a transaction, and answers the row the command returns (`201` for `POST`, `200` otherwise), or `204` when it returns nothing.
264	
265	## Host API (`ctx`), shared by queries and commands
266	
267	| Member | Type | Meaning |
268	| --- | --- | --- |
269	| ``ctx.sql`...` `` | tagged template returning `Sql` | Every `${value}` becomes a bind parameter (`$1`, `$2`, ...), never concatenated text, so it is injection-safe. Values: string, number, boolean, `null`/`undefined` (SQL NULL), arrays of one scalar type (a PostgreSQL array, use `= ANY(${ids})`), or another ``ctx.sql`...` `` fragment, which is inlined with its own parameters. Table and column names cannot be interpolated. |
270	| `ctx.db.query(sql)` | `Row[]` | Runs a `ctx.sql` statement and returns its rows as plain objects (use `RETURNING` to get values back from `INSERT`/`UPDATE`). Synchronous. Inside a command it runs in the command's transaction. |
271	| `ctx.db.exec(sql)` | `{ rowCount }` | Runs a `ctx.sql` statement without returning rows. Synchronous. Passing a plain string is an error. |
272	| `ctx.fetch(url, { method, headers, body })` | `{ status, ok, headers, text(), json() }` | HTTP request to a host listed in `allow.fetch` (`fetch_denied` otherwise). `body` may be a string or an object (sent as JSON). Non-2xx statuses do not throw: check `res.ok`. Synchronous under the hood; `await` works. 5 second timeout. |
273	| `ctx.env(name)` | `string` | Environment variable listed in `allow.env` (`env_denied` otherwise); `""` when unset. For secrets such as API tokens. |
274	| `ctx.reject({ message, pointer?, hint?, code?, status? })` | never returns | Refuses the request with a 4xx problem (commands). |
275	| `ctx.request.method` / `ctx.request.path` | string | HTTP method and path of the request (`"GET"`, `"/books/7"`). |
276	| `ctx.request.query(name)` | `string \| null` | First value of a URL query parameter, `null` when absent. |
277	| `ctx.request.header(name)` | `string \| null` | Request header, case-insensitive, `null` when absent. |
278	| `ctx.operation` | string | `"collection"`, `"item"`, `"create"`, `"update"` or `"delete"`. |
279	| `ctx.id` | `number \| string \| null` | Identifier of the item being read, updated or deleted. |
280	| `ctx.page`, `ctx.itemsPerPage`, `ctx.filters` | number, number, object | Collection requests only (see Queries that return rows). |
281	
282	Request values are strings: cast them in SQL when comparing with non-text columns, otherwise PostgreSQL may fail to infer the type (`query_failed`):
283	
284	```ts
285	export default function query(ctx: QueryContext): Sql {
286	  const since = ctx.request.query("since");
287	  const cond = since === null ? ctx.sql`` : ctx.sql`AND b.year >= ${since}::int`;
288	  return ctx.sql`SELECT b.id, b.title, b.year FROM book b WHERE b.tenant = ${ctx.request.header("x-tenant")} ${cond}`;
289	}
290	```
291	
292	Query parameters that are neither `page` nor a property name are ignored by the server and left to your query (`since` above). Scripts have no other I/O: no imports (except `import { defineResource } from "caddy-resource"`, never needed), no Node.js API, no timers. Type annotations are stripped without type checking; `QueryContext` and `Sql` need no import. A script call must finish within 10 seconds.
293	
294	The query function also runs during validation (`caddy resource validate`, startup, every reload) as a collection request for page 1 with an empty request: no query parameters, no headers (`query()`/`header()` return `null`), `ctx.filters` empty. I/O is switched off there: when the function returns `ctx.sql`, its columns and types are checked with a `LIMIT 0` query; when it calls `ctx.fetch`, `ctx.db.query` or `ctx.db.exec`, validation stops at that call and checks nothing more, and the rows it returns are validated on each request instead (`invalid_row`). Commands are never run during validation.
295	
296	## Starlark scripts (`.star`, `.py`)
297	
298	Starlark is Python without `import`, classes, exceptions (`try`/`except`/`raise`), f-strings, `with`, `async` and the `is` operator; each of those is reported with what to write instead. Strings use `%` or `.format()`, `None` is compared with `==`. The `ctx` API is the same, in snake_case, and every call is synchronous:
299	
300	| TypeScript | Starlark |
301	| --- | --- |
302	| `export default function query(ctx)` | `def query(ctx):` |
303	| `export function create(input, ctx)` / `update` / `remove` | `def create(input, ctx):` / `def update(input, ctx):` / `def remove(input, ctx):` (`def delete` works too) |
304	| ``ctx.sql`... ${a} ... ${b}` `` | `ctx.sql("... {a} ... {b}", a = x, b = y)`: each `{name}` binds the keyword argument of that name (write `/` for literal braces); positional `ctx.sql("... $1 ... $2", x, y)` also works. A value may be another `ctx.sql(...)` fragment |
305	| `ctx.db.query(sql)` / `ctx.db.exec(sql).rowCount` | `ctx.db.query(sql)` / `ctx.db.exec(sql).row_count` |
306	| `await ctx.fetch(url, {method, headers, body})` | `ctx.fetch(url, method = "POST", headers = {...}, body = {...})` |

337	## HTTP API produced
338	
339	Collection, `GET /books?page=2`:
340	
341	```json
342	{
343	  "@context": "/contexts/Book",
344	  "@id": "/books",
345	  "@type": "Collection",
346	  "totalItems": 12,
347	  "member": [
348	    {"@id": "/books/11", "@type": "Book", "id": 11, "title": "Dune", "author": "Frank Herbert"}
349	  ],
350	  "view": {"@id": "/books?page=2", "@type": "PartialCollectionView", "first": "/books?page=1", "last": "/books?page=2", "previous": "/books?page=1"},
351	  "search": {"@type": "IriTemplate", "template": "/books{?author}", "variableRepresentation": "BasicRepresentation", "mapping": [{"@type": "IriTemplateMapping", "variable": "author", "property": "author", "required": false}]}
352	}
353	```
354	
355	- `?page=N` selects a page (1-based); a page after the last one returns an empty `member`. `view` appears when there is more than one page or a filter is applied; `search` when a property is filterable.
356	- `?<property>=<value>` filters on a `filterable` property (exact, case-sensitive match; several filters are combined with AND). Booleans are `true`/`false`, datetimes RFC 3339 or `YYYY-MM-DD`. A non-filterable property is `400 filter_not_enabled`.
357	- Item, `GET /books/11`: the member object plus `"@context": "/contexts/Book"`.
358	- There is no sorting parameter and no partial match.
359	
360	Output formats are chosen, in this order, by a path suffix (`/books.csv`, `/books/7.json`, `.jsonld`), by `?format=jsonld|json|csv`, then by `Accept` (first supported type wins; none or `*/*` gives the first allowed format). A format the resource does not allow (see `formats`) is `406 not_acceptable`, listing the allowed ones.
361	
362	| Format | Media type | Item | Collection |
363	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
364	| `jsonld` (default) | `application/ld+json` | JSON-LD object | Hydra collection above |
365	| `json` | `application/json` | object with the properties only | array of those objects (no total, no links; use `?page=`) |
366	| `csv` | `text/csv` | header row + one row | header row (property names, declaration order) + **every matching row** (filters apply; no pagination unless `?page=N` is given), streamed; NULL is an empty field; sent with `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="<path>.csv"` |
367	
368	Request bodies are JSON only: `Content-Type: application/json`, `application/ld+json` or `application/merge-patch+json` with one JSON object (`415` otherwise; CSV is an output format).
369	
370	Errors are `application/problem+json`:
371	
372	```json
373	{"type": "/errors/422", "title": "An error occurred", "status": 422, "detail": "\"titel\" is not a property of Book", "code": "unknown_property", "hint": "Did you mean \"title\"? The body is validated against \"input\". Accepted keys: title, author_id.", "resource": "Book", "pointer": "/titel"}
374	```
375	
376	When several input errors are found, the first is described at the top level and all of them are listed in an `errors` array (`code`, `pointer`, `message`, `hint` each).

378	## Validation errors
379	
380	`caddy resource validate` prints, and exits with status 1 when `valid` is false:
381	
382	```json
383	{"valid": false, "errors": [{"code": "unknown_column", "resource": "Book", "pointer": "/properties/author", "message": "column \"author\" is not returned by the query", "hint": "Query returns: id, title, author_name. Alias the column in the SELECT (expr AS author) or rename the property."}], "warnings": []}
384	```
385	
386	`resource` is the definition `name` (the file name when the name is unknown), `pointer` is a JSON pointer into that definition. Checks run in this order: JSON syntax / TypeScript compilation, schema, identifier, `table` xor `query`, query and command files and their exports, then, with a dsn, against the database: the table exists, the query runs (empty request), each property is a returned column (or row key), each column type matches. `caddy run` and `caddy validate` do not fail on invalid definitions (only on `Caddyfile` errors such as a missing `dsn`): the server logs the report as a warning and serves the errors on the affected paths.
387	
388	### Error codes
389	
390	| Code | HTTP | When | Fix |
391	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
392	| `command_file_not_found` | 500 | The file named by `command` does not exist next to the definition. | Create it, or fix the file name. |
393	| `conflict` | 409 | A unique constraint rejected the write. | Use a value that does not exist yet. |
394	| `constraint_violation` | 422 | A NOT NULL or CHECK constraint rejected the write. | Send a value for the column named by the pointer, or a value the constraint accepts. |
395	| `database_checks_skipped` | 500 | No dsn was given, so only static checks ran. | Pass --dsn to also check tables, columns and types. |
396	| `database_unreachable` | 503 | PostgreSQL could not be reached with the dsn. | Check host, port, user, password and database name in the dsn. |
397	| `dir_not_found` | 500 | The definitions directory does not exist or is not a directory. | Create it, or fix the `dir` option / --dir flag. |
398	| `duplicate_column` | 500 | The query returns two columns with the same name, or a column reference is ambiguous. | Alias columns so every name is unique (a.id AS author_id). |
399	| `duplicate_name` | 500 | Two definitions share the same `name`. | Rename one of them. |
400	| `duplicate_path` | 500 | Two definitions share the same `path`. | Change one of the paths. |
401	| `env_denied` | 500 | ctx.env read a variable the definition does not allow. | Add the variable name to "allow": {"env": [...]} in the definition. |
402	| `fetch_denied` | 500 | ctx.fetch was called for a host the definition does not allow. | Add the host (or host:port) to "allow": {"fetch": [...]} in the definition. |
403	| `fetch_failed` | 502 | ctx.fetch could not reach the remote server or read its response. | Check the URL and that the remote service is running. |
404	| `filter_not_enabled` | 400 | A query parameter names a property that is not filterable. | Add `"filterable": true` to that property in the definition. |
405	| `internal_error` | 500 | Unexpected server error. | Report it; the message has details. |
406	| `invalid_body` | 400 | The request body is not a JSON object. | Send one JSON object per request. |
407	| `invalid_config` | 500 | The `resource` Caddyfile block is malformed. | Use the options listed in the Caddyfile section (dir, dsn). |
408	| `invalid_export` | 500 | A .ts file has no usable default export. | Definitions: `export default defineResource({...})`. Queries: `export default function query(ctx) {...}`. |
409	| `invalid_filter_value` | 400 | A filter value cannot be converted to the property type. | Send a value matching the property type (integer, number, true/false, RFC 3339 datetime). |
410	| `invalid_json` | 500 | A .json definition is not valid JSON. | Fix the syntax at the reported line/column. |
411	| `invalid_page` | 400 | The `page` query parameter is not a positive integer. | Use ?page=1, ?page=2, ... |
412	| `invalid_parameter` | 400 | A request value could not be converted to the column type inside the query. | Send a value of the right type, or validate it in the query function. |
413	| `invalid_property_value` | 422 | A body value does not match the property type. | Send the JSON type of the property (see the hint). |
414	| `invalid_query_result` | 500 | A query or command function returned a value of the wrong kind. | Queries return a ctx.sql fragment or rows; create returns the new identifier; operation commands return a row or nothing. |
415	| `invalid_reference` | 422 | A foreign key rejected the write: the referenced row does not exist. | Reference an existing row (see the hint for the table). |
416	| `invalid_row` | 500 | A query (or operation command) that returns rows instead of SQL returned a shape or a row that does not match the properties. | Return {items, totalItems} for collections and one row object or null for items; each row needs every property with the declared type. |
417	| `invalid_type` | 500 | A value has the wrong JSON type. | Use the type named in the message. |
418	| `invalid_value` | 500 | A value has the right type but is not allowed (enum, pattern, range). | Use one of the allowed values given in the hint. |
419	| `method_not_allowed` | 405 | Only GET and HEAD are supported on resources. | Resources are read-only in this version. |
420	| `missing_field` | 500 | A required key is missing. | Add the key named in the message. |
421	| `missing_identifier` | 500 | No property has `"identifier": true`. | Mark exactly one property (usually id) as identifier. |
422	| `missing_source` | 500 | Neither `table` nor `query` is set. | Set `table` for a plain table, or `query` for a custom query file. |
423	| `multiple_identifiers` | 500 | More than one property has `"identifier": true`. | Keep exactly one identifier. |
424	| `no_resources` | 500 | The definitions directory contains no definition file. | Add a <Name>.json or <Name>.ts file (see `caddy resource init`). |
425	| `not_acceptable` | 406 | The requested output format (Accept, ?format= or path suffix) is not allowed for this resource. | Use one of the formats listed in the hint, or add the format to "formats" in the definition. |
426	| `not_found` | 404 | No route or no item matches the request. | The hint lists the available paths; item lookups use /<path>/<identifier>. |
427	| `operation_not_supported` | 405 | The command script does not define the function for this operation. | Define `create` (POST), `update` (PUT/PATCH) or `remove` (DELETE) in the command script. |
428	| `permission_denied` | 500 | The database user may not read a table. | Only read from tables the dsn user can SELECT from. |
429	| `query_failed` | 500 | PostgreSQL returned another error while running the query. | Read the message and hint; usually a missing cast on an interpolated value. |
430	| `query_file_not_found` | 500 | The file named by `query` does not exist next to the definition. | Create it, or fix the file name (relative to the definitions directory). |
431	| `query_syntax_error` | 500 | PostgreSQL rejected the query syntax. | Fix the SQL at the reported line/column. |
432	| `read_only_property` | 422 | The body sets a property declared `"readOnly": true`. | Remove it from the body; read-only properties are computed by the query. |
433	| `read_only_resource` | 405 | The resource does not accept writes. | It is `"readOnly": true`, or it uses a `query` without a `command`: add a command file to make it writable. |
434	| `rejected` | 422 | A command rejected the input with ctx.reject(). | Read the message; it is a business rule of the API. |
435	| `required_property` | 422 | A property declared `"required": true` is missing on POST or PUT. | Send it, or use PATCH for a partial update. |
436	| `script_error` | 500 | A script threw an exception or timed out while running. | Fix the script; the message carries the JavaScript error. |
437	| `table_and_query` | 500 | Both `table` and `query` are set. | Keep only one of them. |
438	| `transpile_error` | 500 | A .ts file does not compile. | Fix the TypeScript error at the reported line/column. |
439	| `type_mismatch` | 500 | A column's PostgreSQL type is incompatible with the declared property type. | Change the declared type to the one suggested, or cast in the query (col::text). |
440	| `unknown_column` | 500 | A declared property is not a column of the table or of the query result, or the query references a missing column. | The hint lists the available columns. Alias query columns to the property name. |
441	| `unknown_field` | 500 | A key is not part of the definition schema. | Remove it or use the suggested key; the schema is closed. |
442	| `unknown_property` | 422 | The body contains a key that is not a property of the resource. | Remove it; the hint lists the writable properties. |
443	| `unknown_table` | 500 | A table referenced by `table` or by the query does not exist. | The hint lists the existing tables. |
444	| `unsupported_media_type` | 415 | The request body has a Content-Type the server does not read. | Send a JSON object with Content-Type application/json, application/ld+json or application/merge-patch+json; CSV is an output format only. |
445	| `unused_query_file` | 500 | A *.query.ts file is not referenced by any definition. | Reference it with `query`, or delete it. |
446	
447	Validation codes appear in the report; if they happen at request time (a query failing for a given header value, a fetch denied) they are returned as a problem with the listed status. Codes chosen with `ctx.reject({code})` are not listed here.
